title: FCC Clears SpaceX to Launch 1 Million Starmind Satellites for AI Data Centers in Space
yt_title: FCC Approves 1 MILLION SpaceX Satellites – AI Data Centers in Space!
yt_description:
The FCC just cleared SpaceX to launch up to ONE MILLION satellites for Starmind, a network of AI data centers in orbit. It's the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space. Each satellite has a 75-meter wingspan, runs Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs, and flies between 500 and 1,002 km. Musk talks about a first launch in Q3 2027; the FCC wants the full network by 2040. Astronomers are "disheartened and dismayed." Here's what was approved, why companies want data centers in space, and who else is racing to get there.

script: Welcome to IT News, AI News! Data centers are leaving the planet. Literally. America's FCC just cleared SpaceX to put up to one million satellites in orbit, for a network called Starmind. And these are not internet satellites. Each one is a flying data center, built to run artificial intelligence in space. The FCC calls it the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space. The satellites will fly between five hundred and about one thousand kilometers up, stacked in shells fifty kilometers apart. They are big, too. Each one has a wingspan of seventy five meters. That is wider than a jumbo jet! Inside, SpaceX is working with Nvidia. The Starmind chips use Nvidia Rubin graphics processors and Vera processors. Elon Musk says the first launch could come in the third quarter of twenty twenty seven, with a big ramp up in twenty eight and twenty nine. The FCC deadlines are slower: first satellites by twenty thirty three, half by twenty thirty eight, all of them by twenty forty. For scale: Starlink has about eleven thousand two hundred satellites today. A million is roughly ninety times more! Why space? Fans say orbit solves the land, power and water problems that data centers face on Earth. Critics point at cooling, space traffic and orbital debris. And the FCC demands a detailed debris plan. Astronomers are not happy. The American Astronomical Society says it is disheartened and dismayed, worried about the night sky. The FCC rejected objections from Amazon, Viasat and the astronomers, saying the sky concerns were outside its scope. And SpaceX is not alone. Blue Origin, Starcloud and Google are all chasing their own data centers in orbit. Space is getting crowded! Want the full story? Read it now on itnewsainews dot xpigeon dot net.
